Transportation Research Part F: Traffic Psychology and Behaviour

Volume 91, November 2022, Pages 274-328

Devil in the details: Systematic review of TOR signals in automated driving with a generic classification framework

Author links open overlay panel, , ,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trf.2022.10.009Get rights and content
Under a Creative Commons license
open access

Highlights

  • •

    Take-over requests (TORs) instruct drivers to resume control of an automated vehicle.

  • •

    Detailed understanding how TOR design influences take-over performance is lacking.

  • •

    A novel classification framework was used to systematically review TOR designs.

  • •

    No predominant TOR design exists and detailed information is often not reported.

  • •

    Systematic reporting using the framework enables future meta studies on TOR design.

Abstract

Background

Meta studies on factors contributing to take-over performance did not include the design of take-over request (TOR) signals, other than the modality at which TORs are presented. A detailed understanding of the influence of TOR design on take-over performance is therefore lacking.

Objective

To gain an overview of the level of detail with which TOR designs are reported in academic literature, by using and evaluating a novel classification framework. In this framework TORs are classified in terms of modalities, classes, and underlying attributes. Furthermore, the framework involves classification of potentially competing background signals, as well as the setting in which a study is performed.

Method

A systematic review was performed on articles written in English that were published between 2014 and 2021 using Web of Science, as well as articles retrieved from two previous TOR classification studies and three meta studies on take-over performance. Studies were considered for subsequent analysis if they involved a downward transition of the level of automation following a TOR, resulting in a sample of 391 TORs found in 189 studies.

Results

No predominant TOR design was found, and a considerable part of the available design space has not yet been explored. Studies reported less information on TOR designs when examining TOR designs at an increased level of detail. On average, attribute information was reported for half of the TORs per class.

Conclusions

More attention towards a detailed description of TOR implementations is needed and how this can impact experimental findings. The classification framework and the corresponding coding sheet could support systematic reporting and subsequent meta-analysis in future work. This way, a better understanding about the impact of TOR design on take-over performance can be gained, which in turn can support implementation of safe and effective TORs in (automated) vehicles.

1. Introduction

Developments in automobile technology have been ongoing ever since the first automobile was created. A large trend in recent years has been the effort towards higher levels of automation, with the ultimate goal of a vehicle capable of driving itself under all road conditions without intervention of a driver. Until that stage has been reached, drivers will at some point have to take over control of (parts of) the driving task in case automated technology has been activated. Whether caused by automation failure or by reaching the system’s operational limits, transitions of control are typically signaled by a take-over request (TOR) as part of the vehicle’s human–machine interface (HMI). For traffic safety, it is essential that drivers respond to a TOR by taking over whichever part of the driving task is required, in time (e.g., before a crash is imminent) and with good quality (e.g., appropriate situation awareness of the driver, limited variability in lane position of the vehicle). An important question for scientific researchers, automobile manufacturers and policy makers is how TOR design may optimize take-over performance. Recently, dedicated guidelines on HMI-design for automated vehicles have been introduced (Carsten and Martens, 2019, Naujoks et al., 2019b), which have been verified in terms of usability and user acceptance (e.g., Forster et al., 2020a), but an assessment of the effect of the quality of TOR design on traffic safety is missing.

Take-over time (TOT) and take-over quality (TOQ) following a TOR have been examined in several meta studies (Gold et al., 2018, Zhang et al., 2019, Weaver and DeLucia, 2022). Gold et al. (2018) modelled take-over performance in terms of TOT, time-to-collision (TTC), crash probability, and brake probability, based on six experiments involving SAE level 3 automation (SAE International, 2021) on a three-lane highway. Independent variables were time budget (i.e., available time to take over), traffic density, engagement in non-driving related tasks (NDRTs), repetition, initial lane, and driver age. The resulting models showed a strong influence of time budget, traffic density and repetition on take-over performance, whereas the other independent variables explained a minor portion of the variance in take-over performance. Zhang et al. (2019) focused exclusively on take-over time in their meta-analysis of 129 experimental studies with at least SAE level 2 automation. Out of a set of 18 independent variables, the researchers found that the mean take-over time decreased with a higher urgency of the situation, not using a handheld device, non-involvement in a visual NDRT, repetition of the scenario, and a unimodal auditory or vibrotactile TOR compared to a unimodal visual TOR or the absence of a TOR. Finally, Weaver and DeLucia (2022) performed a meta-analysis on 51 experiments with SAE level 3 automation, in which take-over performance was operationalized in terms of take-over time (i.e., gaze reaction time, road fixation time, hands-on wheel time, and time until the driver’s first general input) as well as take-over quality (i.e., minimum distance, braking magnitude, steering magnitude, lane positioning, number of collisions). Time budget, NDRT engagement, and information support during the takeover (e.g., highlighting the cause of a TOR, recommending a specific response) were coded as independent variables. The analysis showed that a shorter time budget was associated with faster responses on the take-over time measures, but a worse take-over quality. Furthermore, NDRT engagement was associated with longer take-over timing and worse take-over quality. No significant effects of information support (e.g., highlight the cause of a TOR, recommend actions) on response time, nor take-over quality.

In the above meta-analyses the design of a TOR has been considered in terms of time budget (all studies), sensory modality (Zhang et al., 2019), and information support (Weaver & DeLucia, 2022). Other than that, in our view any variation in TOR design has essentially been treated as noise in the statistical analyses, despite various studies suggesting that (more detailed parameters in) TOR design could have an influence on take-over performance. For example, Vlakveld et al. (2018) used a TOR consisting of an auditory alarm in combination with the words ‘take over’ on a display, and suggested that other TOR designs may have shortened the time required for situation awareness to develop. As another example, previous research showing how manipulating the time between pulses (e.g., heartbeats) has been used to successfully convey urgency (van der Heiden et al., 2017, van den Beukel et al., 2016).

If TOR design has not been subjected to statistical modeling at a more detailed level (thus treating details as noise), then the effect of detailed TOR design remains largely unknown, and therefore, there is no reason to believe that those parameters in TOR design have no effect. Gold et al. (2018) report corrected coefficients of determination of 0.43 and 0.63 for the continuous variables TOT and TTC, respectively. This implies that a large part of the variance in the data could not be explained by the independent variables. Zhang et al. (2019) found a strong effect of the study-specific error term, indicating that there are unobserved study variables that affect TOT; a limitation also mentioned by Weaver and DeLucia (2022). If the underlying studies prove to differ largely in terms of how TORs were implemented, then the question arises to what extent more detailed parameters in TOR design may have accounted for (some of the) the unexplained variance in the former meta-analyses.

To investigate the influence of TOR design on TOT and TOQ, one first needs to know if, and at which level of detail TOR designs are described in literature. For this reason, we have performed a systematic review on TOR designs, which was made possible by a novel classification framework postulated below.

1.1. Classification framework

Frameworks can generally be divided in frameworks that are focused on function and frameworks that are focused on form (Cabrall et al., 2016). With a focus on function (e.g., Carsten & Martens, 2019), a framework details the purpose or activity of the human–machine interface (HMI), which a TOR is part of (“why”). Frameworks with a focus on form (e.g., Mirnig et al., 2017, Boelhouwer et al., 2019, Dey et al., 2020) detail the structure, manner or shape of the HMI (“how”). HMI functions may be described in terms of the process or the goals (e.g. inform, warn), whereas HMI forms may be described in terms of quantifiable properties for design and analysis (e.g. modality, size, intensity, location).

A framework for the assessment of specific TOR design choices in improving the automated driving task needs to allow for examining the potential of specific TOR forms. Previous form-based frameworks do not appear to provide enough level of detail to classify implementations of TOR designs encountered in literature. Take, for example, the study of Petermeijer et al. (2017c), who report an auditory TOR involving two single 2700 Hz beeps of 240 ms, spaced at 100 ms, and with a loudness of 80.6 dB. The classification frameworks of Mirnig et al., 2017, Boelhouwer et al., 2019 do not include TOR frequency, duration, or intensity; properties which have been shown to influence perceivability, detectability as well as identifiability (e.g., Nees & Walker, 2011). Therefore, a framework to classify TOR design in more detail is needed, and below we describe why such details may be relevant for takeover performance.

Throughout the following sections, we postulate a form-based framework to classify TOR signals. A takeover situation may involve one or more TOR signals, each of which may be presented through one or more modalities. Within each modality (e.g., visual), one or more classes may be used (e.g., text, symbols), each of which can be described according to a series of attributes (e.g., phrase, color). Thus, TOR signals can be described at three hierarchical levels (see Fig. 1). In addition, background signals (e.g., music, involvement in a non-driving related task), if present, influence the extent with which TOR signals can be detected and discriminated. Finally, setting influences the response to a TOR (e.g., which controls are used to deactivate automation). The ensuing sections provide more details on the blocks depicted in Fig. 1.

1.1.1. Classification based on signal modality

Several frameworks take into account what specific sensory modality would serve a specific function. For example, Drüke et al. (2018) classify HMI design based on the urgency of warnings and interventions and indicate for each level of urgency the sensory modality that might be suitable for communicating about the warning/intervention to the driver. Mirnig et al., 2017, Boelhouwer et al., 2019 categorize HMI design specifically for transitions to another automation level (i.e., following a TOR signal), including the sensory modality that is used to communicate on the transition. Likewise, Dey et al. (2020) include sensory modality in their taxonomy to classify external HMIs of automated vehicles. Furthermore, Naujoks et al. (2019b) developed a checklist to evaluate HMI designs, in which several checklist items pertain to specific sensory modalities. Thus the importance of the sensory modality through which communication takes place has been acknowledged in previous frameworks focusing on form, and moreover, as discussed above, has been shown to influence takeover time (Zhang et al., 2019).

A distinction is typically made between the visual, auditory and tactile modalities (Drüke et al., 2018, Mirnig et al., 2017), as these are the most commonly used modalities for HMIs in automated vehicles (Mirnig et al., 2017). Sometimes smell, taste and vestibular are also being included (Boelhouwer et al., 2019), yet communicating through these modalities is more challenging as perception through these modalities is less precise (Stein, 2012). Moreover, it has been demonstrated that it is not only important to consider unimodal signals (stimulating one of the sensory modalities) but also multisensory signals (stimulating multiple sensory modalities) in HMI design. Multisensory signals can be bimodal (e.g., auditory + visual) or even trimodal (e.g., auditory + visual + tactile). Research has shown that bimodal and trimodal signals can elicit faster responses to critical events during driving than unimodal ones (McNabb, 2017). Moreover, presenting a multisensory instead of an unimodal signal ensures that it is less problematic when a sensory modality of the driver is already taxed (Spence & Ho, 2008). For example, if the driver listens to loud music a signal that is both auditory and tactile will be less likely missed when presenting a signal that is only auditory. Moreover, the brain’s susceptibility to unexpected signals is reduced during driving (Janssen et al., 2019). Therefore, especially for critical notifications it is essential to present a multisensory signal.

The present framework classifies the sensory modality of a TOR in terms of visual, auditory and tactile components, resulting in seven options: unimodal (visual, auditory, tactile), bimodal (visual + auditory, visual + tactile, auditory + tactile) and trimodal (visual + auditory + tactile).

1.1.2. Classification based on signal class

Besides the importance of signal modality and the number of sensory modalities stimulated in TOR design, there are specific signal classes (i.e., types of signals) within a modality that might affect the effectiveness of the communicated information. Previous frameworks (Mirnig et al., 2017, Boelhouwer et al., 2019) for example distinguish between acoustic (beep) sounds and speech sounds to distinguish between differences in length and informational content of speech versus non-speech auditory communication. Likewise, Naujoks et al. (2019b) indicate that complex auditory signals, such as speech output, can convey more detailed information than less complex auditory signals, such as beep sounds. Several signal classes that could be of importance in TOR design have been suggested in the literature and are discussed below for each modality.

Visual classes.

Text is regarded to be a specific type of visual signal (e.g., Dey et al., 2020, Montalvo et al., 2020). Text messages can be less ambiguous than other types of visual signals. Yet, shortcomings of text messages are for example that they are in a specific language and may not be universally understood and that they may not be readable at certain distances (Montalvo et al., 2020).

Anthropomorphic stimuli (using human-like elements for communication, such as facial expressions or gestures) are another specific visual signal class (e.g., Dey et al., 2020). Anthropomorphic representations in HMI design in automated vehicles, compared to non-anthropomorphic representations, have been shown to facilitate trust in and liking of an automated system (Niu et al., 2018). Moreover, Beller et al. (2013) showed that an anthropomorphic stimulus is effective in communicating on automation uncertainty. The benefit of anthropomorphic representations in HMI design is that it can enable untrained users to understand and predict the behavior of a machine (Niu et al., 2018). Yet, phenomena such as the uncanny valley (Mori et al., 2012), in which a human-like stimulus can appear almost human but slightly off and therefore elicits negative emotions, need to be avoided.

Symbols can also be considered as a specific signal class for the visual modality (e.g., Dey et al., 2020, Montalvo et al., 2020). Symbols are visual depictions (not containing human-like elements) that are recognizable and that convey a specific meaning (Dey et al., 2020, Rasmussen, 1983). Examples are an arrow indicating a direction and a red octagon symbolizing there is a need to stop.

Finally, an ‘abstract’ signal class is intended to capture signals that are neither textual, anthropomorphic or symbolic, such as LED bars or illuminated surfaces (following Dey et al., 2020). As described by Dey et al. (2020) these signals would communicate metaphors or these signals would be non-exact and therefore open to interpretation.

Auditory classes.

Speech signals are messages of the human voice, which can be pre-recorded or synthesized on the spot through text-to-speech algorithms. Nees and Walker (2011) argue that speech signals do not require learning (given that one is familiar with the language), but due to their length it may take relatively long to process the intended message. Speech has been used as distinct category in previous classification frameworks for TOR signals (Mirnig et al., 2019), external HMIs (Dey et al., 2020), as well as in guidelines for HMI design (Naujoks et al., 2019b).

Non-speech auditory signals have often been grouped, labeled as, e.g., ‘acoustic’ or ‘abstract’ signals (Mirnig et al., 2019; Dey et al. 2020). However, Nees and Walker (2011) identify several non-speech classes for in-vehicle technologies, each with unique strengths and weaknesses in terms of design flexibility and learnability.

Auditory icons are described as brief, often naturally occurring sounds that have some a priori association with their referent object, event, or process. Examples in the automotive domain range from car horns and skidding tires to signal an imminent collision to bicycle bells and footsteps to warn about the presence of vulnerable road users (Cabral & Remijn, 2019). Auditory icons generally yield faster reactions times and higher response accuracy compared to other non-speech signals described below (Cabral & Remijn, 2019), at times resulting in better performance than established standards (McDougall et al., 2020). Furthermore, they are relatively easily learned and yield a higher user acceptance. However, auditory icons can be misinterpreted when they share the same acoustic characteristics and they are more easily masked by environmental sounds (Cabral & Remijn, 2019).

The ubiquitous ‘beep’ sound is part of the ‘earcon’ class. Lacking an a priori association with its referent (as opposed to auditory icons), earcons can be considered as ‘abstract’ sounds. They often involve rhythms and/or melodies, based on which families of related sounds are created (e.g., two tones with an upward pitch interval to indicate system activation and a downward pitch interval to indicate system de-activation). Other examples fitting within this definition range from sinusoidal tones and frequency modulated tones to tones generated by musical instruments. Earcons are not prone to masking as long as the sound contains harmonics (i.e., no sinusoids), but are relatively difficult to learn and remember due to their abstract nature (Nees & Walker, 2011).

When an auditory signal represents quantitative data, it is called a ‘sonification’ (Nees & Walker). As such, properties of a warning sound are modulated by a phenomenon occurring outside the vehicle. The parking sensor is nowadays a common example: as one’s vehicle gets closer to a parked vehicle, pulses of the auditory signal speed up, an effect reported to increase perceived urgency (van der Heiden et al., 2017, van den Beukel et al., 2016).

Tactile classes.

Within signal classes for the tactile modality we can distinguish vibrational stimuli (Cabrall et al., 2016, Kroon et al., 2019, Naujoks et al., 2019b) and force feedback stimuli (Adell et al., 2008, Yin et al., 2018). Vibrational stimuli are the most commonly applied type of tactile stimuli in HMI design (Naujoks et al., 2019b). Tactile vibrations can for example be embedded in the seatbelt or in the driver’s seat (e.g., McNabb, 2017, Petermeijer et al., 2017a). Intentional force feedback is sometimes used for communicating between the automation and the human driver. For example, Adell et al. (2008) applied a constant force on the accelerator pedal as a warning to support safe speed and safe distance.

1.1.3. Classification based on signal attributes

Each signal class can be described in terms of a series of attributes. Cabrall et al. (2016) even indicate that such a decomposition is necessary for comparing and establishing effects of various HMI implementations on the interaction between driver and automation. Geldard (1960) defined a set of four generic parameters to present information in tactile stimuli: locus, intensity, frequency, and duration. It appears that such parameters are applicable to classes in other modalities as well. For example, Petermeijer et al. (2017c) as well as Politis et al. (2017) present comparable signal implementations across the visual, auditory and tactile modalities, with regards to duration and inter-stimulus interval. Yet, there are also implementation properties specific for a signal modality or class. For example, visual text stimuli include properties such as font type and font style (Naujoks et al., 2019b) that are not applicable to any of the other signal classes. It therefore appears that both generic attributes (applicable to multiple classes) and class-specific attributes should be included in a form-based framework to classify HMI-design.

Generic attributes.

Generic attributes such as signal intensity, inter-pulse interval, onset time, offset time, pulse duration and the number of pulses are able to influence the urgency with which signals are perceived (Naujoks et al., 2019b, van der Heiden et al., 2017, van den Beukel et al., 2016, Marshall et al., 2007), as well as their detectability and identifiability (Cabrall et al., 2016, Nees and Walker, 2011). The guidelines of Naujoks et al. (2019b) appear to use the words ‘burst’ and ‘pulse’ interchangeably, and Nees & Walker (2011) give an example of ‘pulsing bursts centered around 2500 Hz’. For consistent use of terminology, we propose the operationalization depicted in Fig. 2, in line with the definitions in Marshall et al. (2007). Each TOR signal consists of one or more bursts, where each burst has a certain duration and an inter-burst interval in case of multiple bursts. Individual bursts consist of one or more pulses, each with a certain duration, onset time, offset time, frequency, intensity, and an inter-pulse interval in case of multiple pulses.

When, for example, an earcon uses distinct frequencies per pulse, the corresponding TOR will be heard as a melody. In general, the notion of bursts and pulses is applicable to all modalities. Intensity may be interpreted in terms of vibration or force amplitude (tactile signals), loudness (auditory signals) or luminance (visual signals). Likewise, frequency may be interpreted as vibration frequency (vibrotactile signals), pitch (auditory signals), or color (visual signals). Some exceptions apply, which are discussed below for class-specific attributes.

Presentation location is another relevant attribute that applies to all classes. For instance, Politis et al. (2017) demonstrated that a signal presented in a location where the driver’s attention is focused improved response speed, accuracy, and lateral deviation in a handover situation. Furthermore, varying the location of a signal can be employed to attract attention towards a specific direction (McNabb, 2017). Fig. 3 depicts the locations where a TOR signal can be presented. Here it should be noted that although Presentation location as a variable applies to all classes, the set of possible implementations varies between classes. For example, tactile stimuli are unlikely found in the window or on the dashboard, whereas visual stimuli are unlikely found in the seat. Furthermore, in case an experiment is performed using a table-top setup (e.g., with a game steering wheel, one or more screens, and a set of loudspeakers), the locations should be framed as were they part of an actual vehicle interior as depicted in Fig. 3.

Attributes related to timing and location are also very important for multisensory signals. The signals should occur approximately at the same time and approximately in the same location to ensure that signals that stimulate multiple senses are integrated into one percept; this is also called multisensory integration (Stein, 2012). Differences in timing and location can be examined by reporting the TOT and presentation location for each class.

Class-specific attributes.

Class-specific attributes are listed in Table 1. Material is applicable to six classes and describes the shape or sound of the corresponding signal. The set of implementations within Material varies between the classes Symbol (e.g., hands on a steering wheel, foot on a pedal, traffic sign, arrow), Anthropomorphic (e.g., facial expression), Abstract (e.g., circle, square, line, point), Auditory icon (e.g., skidding tires, car horn), and Earcon and Sonification (e.g., sinusoid or pure tone, beep, musical tone, frequency modulated tone). The Material attribute is not applicable to the classes Text and Speech, which by definition can only involve a Phrase (e.g., ‘Take over’, or a countdown timer’10, 9, 8, …, 0′). Following the guidelines of Naujoks et al. (2019b), knowing which phrase has been used helps to determine whether national language was used (for convenience this can be coded as a separate Language attribute), whether simple, non-technical language was used, whether abbreviations were avoided, and whether the phrase refers to functionality of the automation. Likewise, syllable count can be used to assess whether Text and Speech messages are as short as possible. In conjunction with pulse (i.e., phrase) duration, one can determine the Speech rate (for auditory speech signals), an attribute affecting perceived urgency and commandingness (Bazilinskyy & De Winter, 2017). Intonation concerns the pitch contour in Speech (e.g., rising, constant, falling), which has been shown to affect perceived urgency (Ljungberg & Parmentier, 2012). The study by Bazilinskyy and De Winter (2017) suggests that synthesized female voices in a speech signal are easier to understand against a backdrop of noise than male voices. Also, gender of the voice message has been shown to influence the accuracy of responding to route instructions (Jonsson & Dahlbäck, 2011). According to Naujoks et al. (2019b), legibility of text signals is influenced by character spacing, the ratio between stroke width and character height, and the ratio between character width and height. Such properties can be captured through attributes Font type (e.g., Arial, Helvetica) and Font style (e.g., regular, light, condensed). Furthermore, Naujoks et al. (2019b) advice the use of sans-Serif fonts. A separate attribute ‘Font serif’ has been included in the framework, in case the Font name is unknown.

For visual classes, the combination of attributes Width, Height, and Distance to driver allow for determining the visual angle of the signal, which influences its legibility (Naujoks et al., 2019b). Ho et al. (2014) investigated the effect of dynamic tactile cues on brake response time and found that the use of three tactors (i.e., vibration devices) resulted in a faster brake response time compared to using one or two tactors. This finding indicates that a larger vibration area (a specific attribute for the Vibrotactile class) may influence driving performance following a TOR.

Sonification source and destination correspond with the physical phenomenon that causes a change in the sound (e.g., decreasing the distance to a parked vehicle) and the specific auditory attributes affected by the former phenomenon (e.g., reducing the inter-pulse interval). A special case of sonification is looming, where an approaching sound-emitting object is associated with an increase in sound intensity. Gray (2011) found that a looming auditory collision warning resulted in a faster brake response time compared to a non-looming version (i.e., with a static intensity). Moreover, the brake response time increased when the time-to-collision (TTC) signaled by the looming warning was changed from early (compared to the actual TTC) to veridical, to late.

Finally, no class-specific attributes have been introduced for force feedback TOR signals. This class can be described using the generic attributes.

1.1.4. Classification based on background signals

To assess the detectability and discriminability of a TOR, it is necessary to collect information relating to the TOR itself as well as the auditory, visual, and/or tactile background in which the TOR is presented. Detectability concerns whether one can notice that a signal occurred against a background of potentially competing signals. For auditory TORs, a pre-requisite is that the sound is not acoustically masked by other sounds inside the vehicle (such as engine noise). Sinusoid TORs are more easily masked than complex tones with more harmonic content. As a general rule, sounds should be between 15 dB and 30 dB above the background noise (Nees and Walker, 2011, Naujoks et al., 2019b). Likewise, vibrotactile signals should be between 15 dB and 20 dB above the detection threshold for the respective body region (Naujoks et al., 2019b). A visual counterpart of detectability is contrast of foreground and background in terms of luminance and color, for which guidelines are present in Naujoks et al. (2019b). If a signal can be detected, discriminability concerns whether that signal can be discriminated from other signals within and across in-vehicle systems. This can be achieved by avoiding multiple sounds with similar acoustic characteristics, as well as by temporally separating competing sounds by at least 300 ms (Nees & Walker, 2011). For visual signals, Naujoks et al. (2019b) recommend to spatially separate high-priority messages (e.g., TORs) from low-priority messages, but no recommendations on temporal separation are provided. An indication for the impact of one visual signal on subsequent visual signal interpretation may be found in psychophysics, where slow adaptation to intensity fluctuations in sensory system cells has been shown to last around 10000 ms (Baccus & Meister, 2002).

Aside from background noise and signals (visual, auditory, tactile) generated by in-vehicle systems, experimental studies often employ non-driving related tasks (NDRTs) which may involve signals affecting the detectability and/or discriminability of a TOR. Moreover, meta studies have shown that NDRT engagement negatively influences take-over timing and take-over quality (Zhang et al., 2019, Weaver and DeLucia, 2022). Potential masking effects resulting from NDRT-signals should be taken into account when investigating the effect of TOR design on takeover performance.

Based on the above guidelines and observations, the present framework accommodates an assessment of detectability and discriminability as follows. For TORs with a visual component, the presence of (NDRT-)signals is coded within the time window running from 10000 ms prior to the TOR onset to the moment at which the driver takes over or has to take over. We expect that signals presented and ending before this time window are unlikely to influence TOR detectability and discriminability. Spatial and temporal proximity are defined as the minimum distance and minimum time between any of these signals and the TOR signal, respectively. TORs with an auditory component are coded with the same properties as TORs with a visual component. In addition, the presence of stationary background noise (e.g., engine noise, road noise, wind and rain noise, music) and its intensity are included. Finally, the presence of tactile NDRT and background noise, as well as the intensity of background noise are coded for TORs with a tactile component.

1.1.5. Classification based on setting

The categorization framework of Mirnig et al. (2017) on control transition interfaces lists several take-over properties that cannot be attributed to the TOR signal itself (e.g., modality, class, attributes) or background signals:

  • •

    Direction: concerns whether a take-over (i.e., from system to driver) and/or a hand-over (i.e., from driver to system) takes place.

  • •

    Initiation: is the transition initiated by the user, system, or both?

  • •

    Involvement: does the vehicle ask the driver to conform that the requested control has been taken back?

  • •

    Completeness: are all driving and monitoring functions transferred at once, or incrementally, or partially?

  • •

    Fallback: system strategies in case a transition is unsuccessful (e.g., stopping in the ego lane or in another lane).

  • •

    Input modality concerns how a driver can respond to a TOR (e.g., physical, touch, speech, gestures).

  • •

    Mode awareness: features used by the vehicle to inform the driver about the system state before the TOR (e.g., text, symbols, colors, audio).

These properties may shape the way drivers respond to TORs (and influence how designers implement TORs) and are therefore labelled as ‘setting’ in the present framework.

Higher levels of automated driving give rise to new human factor issues (Carsten & Martens, 2019) and therefore it is important to consider the specific automated driving level(s) that are activated during communication of a signal when assessing the HMI’s effectiveness. This can be interpreted in more ways than what has been done in previous meta studies (Gold et al., 2018, Zhang et al., 2019, Weaver and DeLucia, 2022), which seem to focus solely on transitions from either partial, conditional, or highly automated (i.e., SAE level 2 and above) to manual driving (i.e., SAE level 0). Lu et al. (2016) postulate a driver-automation system with six states, each with a distinct distribution of responsibilities between the driver and automation in terms of three primary driving tasks: lateral control, longitudinal control, and monitoring. Furthermore, Lu et al. (2016) discern between two transition types between the states of the driver-automation system. First, ‘control transitions’ are transitions in which the execution of at least one control task changes between driver and automation (e.g., from level 3 to level 0 when interpreted in terms of the SAE levels of automation). Second, ‘monitoring transitions’ are transitions in which only the required monitoring frequency changes between driver and automation (e.g., from level 4 to level 2). A transition can take place in either direction, whereas a take-over has been framed as a transition from a high to a low level of automation, the latter typically manual driving (Mirnig et al., 2017, Zhang et al., 2019). Lu et al. (2016) state that a take-over may be initiated by an exceedance of the automation’s operational limits. Take-overs have mostly been studied as control transitions, but the exceedance of the automation’s operational limits could also refer to its monitoring abilities in a particular context. Likewise, take-over requests (TORs), which have been used mostly for control transitions, may also be used to signal monitoring transitions (e.g., Forster et al., 2020b). Furthermore, several measures relevant for studying control transitions are likely also relevant for monitoring transitions, such as gaze reaction time and hands-on-wheel time. The present framework therefore includes TORs for control transitions, as well as monitoring transitions.

Setting also involves properties situated outside the vehicle. Previous meta studies show that traffic density influences take-over timing and take-over quality (Gold et al., 2018, Zhang et al., 2019). Therefore, traffic density is included in the present framework such that the effect of traffic density can be controlled for in a future meta study on the effect of TOR design on take-over performance.

1.2. Study objective

The classification framework presented above serves two aims: 1) to support systematic reporting of TOR design parameters in future studies, and 2) to support inventorying of TOR design parameters used in previous studies. The framework includes a hierarchical classification of TOR signals at three levels: 1) modality or modalities through which the signal is presented, 2) classes within a modality in which the signal falls, and 3) description of those classes according to attributes. Additionally, the framework considers background signals and the experimental context which is thought to shape the interaction with a TOR signal. The framework is a valuable addition to previous work that mostly considered (more detailed) TOR design as noise in statistical analyses. The impact of TOR design on take-over performance is currently unclear. Moreover, if one wants to gain insight into the effects of TOR design the design space should be explored broadly. It is currently also unclear how much of the design space has been employed in previous studies.

A logical next step is to apply the proposed framework in order to create an inventory of TOR implementations in previous studies. The goal of such an inventory is to gain insight into the utilized design space and, ultimately, to establish effects of specific aspects of TOR design through future meta-analyses. An important prerequisite to reach these goals is that details considered in the framework are actually reported in previous work. Therefore, first it needs to be established to what degree implementation of TOR design can be deduced from previous research in order to determine whether insights can be gained into the utilized design space and whether meta-analyses will be meaningful. We next present a systematic review in which the framework has been used to categorize previous experimental studies.

2. Method

A systematic literature search was performed using the framework postulated above, to examine at which level of detail TOR designs have been reported in literature. This study is reported conforming to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). The PRISMA checklist is available in Appendix A. No protocol was generated or registered.

2.1. Information sources & search strategy

Studies used in the frameworks of Mirnig et al., 2017, Boelhouwer et al., 2019, as well as the meta-analyses of Gold et al., 2018, Zhang et al., 2019, and Weaver and DeLucia (2022) were selected for subsequent screening (see below). In addition, a literature search was performed in Web of Science using a query with two keyword groups in the topic field. Group one consisted of ‘selfdriving’, ‘autonomous’, ‘automated’, ‘self-driving’, and ‘self driving’. Group two consisted of ‘handover’, ‘hand-over’, ‘hand over’, ‘takeover’, ‘take-over’, ‘take over’, and ‘transition’. Keywords within each keyword group were connected with logical ‘OR’ operators, whereas the keyword groups were connected with a logical ‘AND’ operator. The language of the query was set to English, including articles, early access, as well as proceedings papers for publications between 2014 and 2021. Included indexes were SCI expanded, SSCI, A&HCI, BKCI-S, BKCI-SSH, and ESCI.

We deliberately chose to include proceedings papers to yield an as large as possible sample, but acknowledge that especially proceedings papers may suffer from selective reporting of TOR implementation details due to restrictions on the manuscript length. The query was performed on March 30th 2021. Together with the papers derived from the meta-analyses, a total initial sample of 719 papers was subjected to the screening process described in the next sections.

Production cars were not considered in the present review. Mirnig et al. (2017) note that it is difficult to keep track of the exact implementation of signals related to autonomous driving technologies, due to rapid changes in their development. Also, today’s production cars are not (yet) legally allowed to use automation beyond level 2, and cars with level 3 automation have been introduced only recently (e.g., Templeton, 2021), which means very few examples of TOR signals are expected. Industry patents were deliberately excluded, too. Patents do not require a fully working implementation, and may cover several different implementation concepts to secure a market advantage (Mirnig et al., 2017). This reduces the likelihood of unambiguously coding the implementation of TORs covered by industry patents; a necessity in the present review.

2.2. Eligibility criteria

Studies had to fulfill the following five criteria to be included in this review:

  • 1.

    The study had to involve a control transition or monitoring transition from partially, conditionally, or highly automated driving (i.e., SAE levels of automation 2–4; hands off the steering wheel and feet off the pedals) to any lower level of automation (i.e., SAE levels of automation 0–3).

  • 2.

    The study had to involve a transition in response to a ‘take-over request’ (TOR). That is, we included only ‘mandatory automation initiates driver-in-control (AIDC) transitions’ as defined by Lu et al. (2016).

  • 3.

    The TOR had to be implemented physically, as opposed to a hypothetical TOR that had to be imagined (e.g., Bazilinskyy & De Winter, 2015).

  • 4.

    Excluded were non-English language studies, studies that did not describe automation technology in cars, reviews, commentaries, and studies of which the full article was not accessible.

  • 5.

    Following Mirnig et al. (2017), only publications starting from 2014 were considered, as this year coincides with the first publication of the NHTSA (late 2013) and SAE (early 2014) levels of driving automation.

2.3. Study selection & data extraction

Identification of 774 records resulted in a final set of 189 included studies, as follows (see Fig. 4). First, duplicate records were removed from the initial sample identified through database and literature search, based on the combination of authors, manuscript title and publication year. Based on the reference and additional details provided by Web of Science, records which proved to be non-English, and/or published before 2014 were removed. The remaining records were distributed across the four authors to verify whether a report met the eligibility criteria (i.e., each report was screened by one author). Screening started with the title and abstract. The full paper was assessed in case not all eligibility criteria could be verified. When a report proved to disagree with any of the eligibility criteria listed in the previous section, the report was not further screened on the remaining eligibility criteria. No steps were taken to avoid double counting due to different reports of the same study (e.g., published in another year under another title). Thus, each report has been treated as a unique study. This approach was chosen to provide the best possible insight into the deducibility of TOR design parameters as they are encountered in individual publications.

A codebook (see Appendix B) was developed based on the classification framework presented in Section 1.1. The codebook was operationalized in Microsoft Excel (v2203), offering separate sheets for instructions, background signals and setting, as well as seven separate sheets for all combinations of the visual, auditory and tactile TOR modalities. Within each of those seven sheets maximally-four distinct TORs could be coded. This setup was based on an initial survey of studies used in the meta-analysis of Zhang et al. (2019), where Politis et al. (2017) proved to be the study with the largest number of distinct TORs: 28 in total; 4 TORs per modality sheet. The operationalized codebook was pilot-tested on two studies randomly selected from the sample, and refined accordingly. Studies were coded in-depth by authors RJJ, SvdK, and RdZ. Only information reported within a study was considered; corresponding authors were not contacted and no snowballing techniques were used to derive additional information in case references to previous experimental setups were made. However, note was taken of studies providing such references.

2.4. Analysis methods

Analysis of the coded papers has been performed for each of the blocks in the hierarchical framework depicted in Fig. 1. From this framework, it follows that TOR classes can only be examined when the corresponding TOR modality is implemented. Likewise, TOR attributes can only be examined when the corresponding TOR class is implemented. As will be shown, a key observation of our analysis is that variables in the codebook were often found unreported in the studies under scrutiny. To provide insight into the number of missing values in the following analysis, we report the proportion of ‘deducible’ values for each variable in the codebook. Deducibility here refers to whether a study provides any information about a variable (e.g., a unimodal visual TOR was used), including information based on which the absence of an implementation could be determined (e.g., the TOR did not involve an auditory component). It follows that deducibility of a variable (e.g., a TOR phrase in case text is used) involves the entire sample (i.e., including TORs in which the phrase is coded as ‘unknown’). When reporting proportions of ‘known’ categories within a variable, however, cells coded as ‘unknown’ are left out of the equation. In other words, other than deducibility, reported counts and proportions regarding TOR implementation represent only the ‘known’ subset of the sample.

A dedicated R-script was written to process the Excel sheets with coded studies, to show the coders which entries were overlooked, and ultimately to verify that all applicable fields were entered. The base package (version 4.1.1) was used to calculate proportions, means and standard deviations. Package ‘ggplot2′ (version 3.3.5) was used for visualizations.

In terms of implementation of TOR attributes (which turned out to show a relatively low deducibility), we focus on attributes of which a value is known in at least 50 % of the corresponding class. Furthermore, we distinguish between attributes with low variability (3 or fewer unique categories, or a dominant category) and attributes with high variability (>3 unique categories without a dominant category) to describe the range of the design space used. The rationale for these thresholds is that if an attribute with a deducibility of 50 % involves a single unique category or value, then a theoretical deducibility of 100 % would result in at least one dominant category. Conversely, if an attribute with a deducibility of 50 % involves a large number of unique categories without a dominant category, then a theoretical deducibility of 100 % unlikely results in one or two dominant categories. Thus, using a criterion of 50 % deducibility yields insights in the potential variability in the full TOR population, which in turn may inform the number of categories required in future meta studies.

Interrater reliability was assessed before and after coding of the studies, and is described in more detail in Appendix D.

3. Results & discussion

3.1. Sample description

A total of 391 distinct TORs were coded within the sample of 189 studies (see Appendix C). Studies with more than one TOR were due to manipulations of the TOR implementation (e.g., Politis et al., 2017) or because multiple TORs were presented in a single takeover situation (e.g., Forster et al., 2017). The majority of studies did not refer to other studies when describing a TOR implementation. Of the 27 studies with such references, all of which were included in the final sample, 18 studies (jointly accounting for 92 distinct TORs) involved an ambiguous reference, in that the TOR implementation was reported as an adjustment from earlier work (e.g., Politis et al., 2015), based on earlier work (e.g., Stanton et al., 2022) or guidelines (e.g., Wan & Wu, 2018a), or in line with previous work (e.g., Borojeni et al., 2016). The other 9 studies (involving a total of 20 TORs) explicitly stated that the TOR implementation was a copy from earlier work (Müller et al., 2021, Petermeijer et al., 2017c, Naujoks et al., 2014, Sportillo et al., 2018) or that more details about the TOR implementation could be found in earlier work (Forster et al., 2016, Forster et al., 2017, Körber et al., 2016b, Naujoks et al., 2017b, Wiedemann et al., 2018).

The coding scheme constructed for the present study allowed for a maximum of 4 distinct TORs per modality. In one paper (Chen et al., 2020) there were 5 settings for the takeover time (TOT), which required coding 5 TORs. In this case one TOT-setting was omitted. Another paper (Duthoit et al, 2017) tested 15 distinct tactile TORs, of which only four could be coded. Thus, a total of 12 TORs were identified, but not coded. For both papers, care was taken to select TORs that would cover the widest area of the design space. Furthermore, the coding scheme allowed for a maximum of 4 distinct frequencies (i.e., one per pulse) so that, e.g., short melodies can be included. One paper described a TOR with 8 pulses (Borojeni et al., 2018b). Seeing that the same frequency was used 8 times, the first four frequencies were coded and the remaining ones were omitted.

3.2. TOR modalities

3.2.1. Deducibility

Five studies stated that a TOR was presented to the driver without providing details on the modality of the TOR (Scharfe et al., 2020, Lee et al., 2021, Jarosch et al., 2017, Ebnali et al., 2019, Körber et al., 2016b). In two of these studies, a time budget was specified, but this could not be coded as attribute lacking information about modality and class. The modality of each TOR was deducible in the remaining 184 studies, resulting in a deducibility of modality in 386 (or 98.7 % of the) TORs. Note that a high deducibility here involves both unambiguous presence and absence of a modality.

3.2.2. Implementation

A total of 386 TORs were coded on modality. Fig. 5 shows how TORs were distributed across the modalities. All unimodal and multimodal TORs were represented in the sample of studies. A multimodal visual-auditory TOR was by far the most common implementation (44.3 %), followed by a unimodal auditory TOR (22.5 %). This finding is in line with Boelhouwer et al. (2019), where visual-auditory and auditory TORs were the largest groups, too, constituting 35.5 % and 19.4 % of the total number of TORs, respectively. In contrast, the largest TOR groups in Mirnig et al. (2017) were visual-auditory (42.9 %) and visual (22.9 %), with auditory TORs accounting for a mere 5.7 % of the sample. Thus, recent studies may have more often employed auditory TORs.

3.3. TOR classes

3.3.1. Deducibility

Several studies reported the modality of a TOR, but failed to indicate which class was implemented. Consequently, the deducibility of class ranged between 84.3 % and 89.5 % across the classes (M = 87.1, SD = 1.9). In some cases, lack of information on class meant that additional information at the attribute level could not be coded, for example: “Sounds are also emitted, especially-one for takeover, that lasts during the whole transition phase and is designed to sound more and more urgent.” (Langlois et al., 2016).

3.4. Implementation

Looking at the actual implementation of TOR classes in Fig. 6, text and symbols are most often used in TORs with a visual component, whereas earcons (and to a lesser extent speech) are mostly used in TORs with an auditory component. Visual anthropomorphic, auditory sonification, and tactile force feedback classes were not observed in the sample. A comparison with previous studies classifying TOR designs (Mirnig et al., 2017, Boelhouwer et al., 2019) cannot be made regarding these classes, because they were not included in the corresponding frameworks.

TORs may involve multiple classes. We observed 41 distinct implementations of (combinations of) classes in the sample. Fig. 7 depicts the frequency of class implementations per modality. For unimodal auditory as well as bimodal auditory-tactile TORs, earcons and speech are the most occurring classes, yet they are seldomly used together, in line with findings by Boelhouwer et al. (2019). The earcon-speech combination is found in 4 unimodal auditory TORs (accounting for 3.8 % of the modality) and in 8 bimodal visual-auditory TORs (6.9 %). For unimodal visual TORs text is most often used exclusively (25 TORs; 32.4 % of the visual modality), followed by a combination with symbols and abstract shapes (8 TORs; 21.6 %). The bimodal visual-auditory TORs and the trimodal visual-auditory-tactile TORs have been implemented in a large number of combinations of text, symbols, abstract shapes, speech, earcons, and vibrations, and consequently show frequencies ranging between 1 and 25 TORs. All in all, the most frequently occurring modality (i.e., bimodal visual-auditory) does not show a predominant implementation in terms of classes, whereas the second most frequently occurring modality (i.e., unimodal auditory) features two common implementations, involving either speech or earcons.

3.5. TOR attributes

3.5.1. Deducibility

Several studies mentioned the modality and class of a TOR, but did not specify the underlying attributes, such as what type of sound was used, as well as its frequency, intensity and duration (e.g., Vogelpohl et al., 2020, Vlakveld et al., 2018). Fig. 8 displays the deducibility of attributes in three visual classes, regardless of the modality in which the class was used (e.g., unimodal, bimodal, trimodal). Likewise, Fig. 9 displays the deducibility of attributes for the classes speech, earcons and vibration. Auditory icons have been excluded from subsequent analysis at the attribute level, because there were only 3 instances, all reported by a single study (van den Beukel et al., 2016). The mean deducibility across attributes within a class ranged between 42.1 % (auditory earcons) and 58.1 % (visual abstract), with a grand mean of M = 50.5 % (SD = 5.3) across all classes presented in Fig. 8 and Fig. 9.

Temporal attributes have been coded in all classes. In terms of the signal repetition (i.e., burst count, pulse count), the deducibility ranged between 60.9 % and 73.9 % (M = 66.4 %, SD = 4.1) for all classes shown in Fig. 10 and Fig. 11. Inter-burst interval and inter-pulse interval were coded in case at least two bursts or pulses were reported, yielding a deducibility above 70.6 % for all classes, except for earcons (50.0 % and 52.6 %, respectively). For example, Geitner et al. (2019) report “a 2 s beep […] pulsing seven times”, and van der Heiden et al. (2017) report a TOR implementation in which “bursts of 3 beeps are played 3 times, with silence in between burst sets”. In both examples the authors did not specify the duration of the pause between the beeps. In terms of duration (i.e., burst duration, pulse duration and total signal duration), the deducibility ranged between 10.0 % and 77.9 % (M = 37.9 %, SD = 18.1). Notably, the deducibility was below 52 % for visual and auditory classes, and above 60 % for the tactile vibration class. Finally, takeover time could be deduced in 56.3 % to 84.8 % across the classes (M = 69.4 %, SD = 11.5).

Location has also been coded in all classes. For visual and tactile classes the location was generally reported (deducibility between 71.9 % and 98.5 %). In contrast, studies did not often report where auditory signals were presented (19.6 % for speech; 35.4 % for earcons). Regarding the implementation of TORs, the types of imagery and sound used (or phrases in case of text and speech) were generally well-reported (M = 89.0 %, SD = 3.9). For visual classes the signal color(s) and the color of the surface on which the signal was displayed could on average be deduced in 79.5 % of the TORs (SD = 13.1). However, height, width, and distance were typically unreported, in which case the signal’s angular size cannot be calculated. For text specifically, font type and font style were not reported in any of the studies, and could not be deduced based on photographs provided in the studies (which typically did provide enough detail to identify whether a serif font was used).

For auditory speech and earcons, as well as tactile vibration the signal intensity and its development over time were mostly unreported (M = 6.3 %, SD = 7.1), as a result of which the signal-to-noise ratio cannot be determined. Furthermore, earcon and vibration signals were not described in terms of onset and offset duration. The frequencies at which they were heard or felt were frequently omitted in the reporting (deducible in 42.4 % and 44.1 %, respectively). For speech signals, gender was reported in 36.6 % of the TORs, but intonation was not mentioned at all. Only one study (Petermeijer et al., 2017b) mentioned the size of the vibration sensors and their interspacing, based on which the vibration size could be calculated.

3.5.2. Implementation

Originally, a joint total of 88 unique phrases were found within the classes visual text and auditory speech, many of which are highly similar (e.g., ‘Take over’, ‘Take over!’, ‘Takeover’, and the German counterpart ‘Ubernehmen’). Phrases with a similar meaning were clustered to reduce the number of categories. A phrase typically consisted of one or more elements of the following building blocks: [alert][reason][please][take over][control][immediacy][action]. For example, the phrase “Danger! Collision imminent you have control!” (Politis et al., 2017) was categorized as [alert][reason][take over][control] and the phrase “Alert! Take over vehicle control now!” (Roche et al., 2018) was categorized as [alert][take over][control][immediacy]. Alternatively to the above building blocks, phrases could concern a countdown (e.g., Wintersberger et al., 2018) or simply an action (e.g., “Press X” in Brandenburg & Chuang, 2019).

The color of a visual TOR and the pulse frequency of auditory and tactile TORs could be coded with up to three values. Signal color and signal color count were respectively calculated as all unique color combination and the number of colors used simultaneously. Signal frequency and signal frequency count were respectively calculated as all unique frequency combinations and the number of distinct frequencies used across pulses within a TOR. No differentiation was made between upward and downward frequency shifts (e.g., melodies in case of an earcon).

In the following, we focus on single attributes within each class, because the large number of unreported attributes impedes examination of combinations of attributes (as illustrated in Fig. 7 for classes). Only attributes of which a value is reported (deducible) in at least 50 % of the corresponding class are considered. Attributes of the visual text class are represented as circles in Fig. 10 (other classes are illustrated in Appendix E). The number of unique values in each attribute was calculated to obtain an initial overview of the degree of variability within each class. Certain attribute values have been used in very few studies (e.g., Pulse count: 7, N = 1), whereas other values have been re-used across several studies (e.g., Pulse count: 1, N = 79). Thus, the number of unique values alone is not enough to understand how the potential design space has been covered. Indicative for the distribution of unique values, the vertical axis in Fig. 10 shows the value with the largest proportion.

An attribute with at least two unique values can be said to have a dominant value if the value with the largest proportion covers>50 %. Marked by a dashed red line in Fig. 10, we distinguish between attributes with low variability (=less than3 unique values, or a dominant value) and attributes with high variability (>3 unique values and no dominant value). Table 2 presents an overview of the variability of attributes across classes after applying the same criterion to the other classes (see Appendix E). Such information may be helpful in future meta-studies when considering certain attributes as factors. For example, phrase may be difficult to operationalize as dichotomous variable, whereas language may feature too little variability to perform inferential statistics.
