Four attributes only showed a low variability. Across all classes, a burst count of 1 has been reported exclusively (text, symbol, abstract, speech), or almost exclusively (earcon: 98.1 %, vibration: 95.9 %). Consequently, burst interval only applied to one earcon (t = 14000 ms) and three TORs with vibration (twice at t = 800 ms and once at t = 1800 ms). Phrases were predominantly reported in English for speech (96.6 %) and text (82.9 %). It should be noted that phrases were occasionally reported in English, even when non-English participants were recruited. This raises the question to which extent the actual phrase language (e.g., German) was biased by the language in which the manuscript was published (i.e., English). Within TORs with a text class, 98.8 % used a sans serif font.

Seven attributes only showed a high variability. Takeover time met this criterion in all classes and showed between 11 and 26 unique values (see Appendix E). The average takeover time per class ranged between M = 7000 ms for earcons (SD = 4970) and M = 11470 ms for vibration (SD = 16560). Regarding signal color, TORs with texts were often, but not dominantly, red (34.0 %) or white (35.9 %), and likewise, TORs with abstract visuals were often red (42.2 %). For symbolic TORs unicolor red was the most common implementation (24.0 %), followed by a combination of black and white (16.7 %). The most common pulse durations in abstract TORs were 100 ms and 250 ms (M = 5045 ms, SD = 9756). For TORs with tactile vibration, pulse durations of 200 ms were often found (M = 254 ms, SD = 184), but not enough to consider it a dominant implementation. Burst duration (M = 3735 ms, SD = 5662) and total duration (M = 8039 ms, SD = 10188) also showed high variability in vibration TORs, but did not meet the criterion for deducibility in other classes. Phrase showed a high variability: the four (text) and five (speech) largest phrase categories constituted the first 50 % of the reported phrases. These phrase categories were: [take over], [please][take over], [take over][control], [alert][reason] (speech only), and [alert][reason][take over][control]. As a result, the number of syllables in speech also showed a high variability. Ranging between 1 and 22 syllables, the most occurring value was 5 syllables (14.4 %), followed by 12 syllables (13.3 %).

Finally, six attributes showed high variability in some classes and low variability in other classes. Starting with pulse count, a single pulse is mostly found in symbols (93.2 %), speech (91.4 %), and text (82.2 %), occasionally alternated with 2 or 3 pulses (symbols and speech) or a larger series of pulses (text) associated with countdown timers (e.g., Wu et al., 2019b). A relatively large variety in pulse count is found for classes abstract (1: 56.4 %, 8: 25.6 %), earcon (1: 46.2 %, 2: 27.4 %, 8: 8.5 %) and vibration (1: 28.9 %, 3: 31.1 %, 8: 17.8 %). All TORs with 8 pulses were implemented by Politis et al. (2017), indicating that a single study played a relatively large role in the variability of pulse count. The pulse interval was exclusively 0 ms for text and symbol TORs and dominantly 100 ms for abstract (62.5 %) and earcon (63.6 %) TORs. In vibration TORs 100 ms was the most occurring value, but it was not dominant (38.5 %, M = 180 ms, SD = 161). In speech TORs, no single pulse interval value occurred more than once (M = 6800 ms, SD = 2864). Regarding location, on the one hand TORs with vibration were situated mainly in the chair (71.6 %), followed at a distance by wristbands (26.9 %) and the steering wheel (1.5 %). On the other hand, visual TORs showed a larger variability, where at least two (symbols) or three (text, abstract) categories were required to make up for 50 % of the reported locations (typically involving the center console, windshield, instrument cluster, Head Up Display (HUD), or a combination of these). In terms of material, dominant categories were found at symbols, which mostly involved hands placed on a steering wheel (59.6 %) followed by a combination of symbols (17.3 %, e.g., hands on wheel and foot on pedal), and at earcons, typically consisting of unspecified ‘beeps’ or ‘tones’ (75.4 %) followed by sinusoids (18.1 %). TORs with an abstract class, on the other hand, did not feature a dominant category: line (25.0 %), circle (20.0 %), rectangular (11.7 %), point (11.7 %), other (31.7 %). Regarding the number of signal colors, text (100 %) and abstract (71.9)%) TORs typically featured one signal color (71.9 %) (i.e., low variability). Unicolor, bicolor and tricolor showed similar proportions in symbolic TORs (high variability). TORs with an abstract class mostly featured a transparent background color (67.4 %), whereas text and symbols involved eight different colors; black (31.5 % and 35.6 %, respectively), red (26.1 % and 15.1 %) and transparent (25.0 % and 19.2 %) being the largest categories.

3.6. Background signals

Background signals were coded in terms of NDRT-involvement (for each study) and in terms of non-NDRT-related signals (separately for each modality if used within a TOR). The deducibility of background signals is presented in Fig. 11, with an average of M = 43.7 % (SD = 40.9). In general, the presence of NDRT-involvement could be well deduced, although auditory NDRT-involvement proved to be more difficult to derive than visual and tactile NDRT-involvement. For example, when participants had to play a game on a tablet, it was often unclear if the game used audio and whether the tablet emitted those sounds. If deducible, visual, auditory, and/or manual (tactile) NDRT-tasks were performed in at least one experimental condition in 85.2 %, 38.1 %, and 72.6 % of the studies, respectively.

Presence of visual background signals (aside from NDRT-related signals) could be deduced in 36 studies featuring a TOR with a visual component (27.3 %), within which 26 studies with at least one visual background signal was identified. For example, in Naujoks et al. (2015) visual-auditory TORs related to a traffic jam assist were accompanied by visual cues indicating the status of several subcomponents of the traffic jam assist. These signals were subsequently coded on whether a background signal was related to vehicle automation (as was the case in the example of Naujoks et al., 2015), as well as Spatial and Temporal proximity in relation to the TOR location and timing. A relation with vehicle automation was deducible in 24 out of 26 visual background signals, and true for 20 signals. Spatial proximity was deducible in 6 signals, always showing a distance of 0 cm. Here it should be noted that distances other than 0 cm could not be derived based on photographs of the experimental setup, resulting in an’unknown’ value. Temporal proximity was deducible in 19 signals, always coinciding with the TOR.

The auditory background was coded in terms of noise (e.g., engine, road, wind) and in terms of non-NDRT signals (e.g., automation status messages). Occasionally studies reported which sound system was used as part of a driving simulator setup (e.g., Bourelly et al., 2019). Seeing that a driving simulator can be configured by the experimenter, including which sounds are presented to a participant, auditory background signals were only coded when explicitly mentioned. Consequently, noise was deducible and present in 44 studies featuring a TOR with an auditory component (26.3 %). Noise intensity was reported in 2 of those 44 studies, namely engine noise of 60 dB (van den Breukel et al., 2016) and road noise of 50 dB (Mok et al., 2017). In 9 studies where a TOR included an auditory component it was possible to deduce whether an auditory (non-NDRT, non-noise) background signal was present (5.4 %), which was the case in 5 studies. For as far as could be deduced, in 2 studies the corresponding signal(s) had a relation with automation, and in two other studies it did not. Presentation location and timing, and hence spatial and temporal proximity, could not be deduced.

None of the 28 studies reporting a TOR with a tactile component provided information about the intensity of tactile background noise.

Detectability and discriminability of a TOR signal cannot be assessed when studies do not report the presence and intensity of background signals, or fail to report the intensity of a TOR signal (see above). This lack of information was found in the majority of the studies. It should be noted however, that a small portion of the studies did report about the detectability of a TOR without explicitly stating the signal and background intensity. For example, Li et al. (2020) did not report the loudness of an auditory TOR and its background, but did report the TOR was loud enough to be perceived over entertainment video sounds. The coding sheets could not account for such descriptions in the present study, resulting in missing values. Adjustment of the coding scheme may be required for a future inventory.

Another observation is that studies reporting (background) signal intensity mostly expressed intensity in the acoustical unit dB, but Politis et al. (2015) used the electronical unit dBFS. The latter unit does not provide an indication on the intensity with which participants heard the TORs. Furthermore, studies expressing intensity in dB did not report where such measurements were taken (e.g., at the listening position), nor how such measurements were obtained (with notable exceptions found in Petermeijer et al., 2016 and Petermeijer et al., 2017c). Consequently, the validity of a comparison of TOR intensities across studies is unknown.

3.7. Setting

Deducibility of the setting variables fluctuated between 41.3 % and 98.9 % (M = 80.0 %, SD = 20.8), see Fig. 12. TORs were often (N = 107, corresponding with 80.5 % of the deducible sample) issued in presence of other traffic in the neighboring lane(s). Traffic density, expressed as the number of vehicles per kilometer (following the meta-analysis of Gold et al., 2018), could be derived in 20 studies. Several studies used alternative measures, such as a qualitative indication (e.g., ‘moderate traffic conditions’ in Eriksson et al., 2017c) or the number of vehicles per hour (e.g., Lin et al., 2020, Wu et al., 2020, Vogelpohl et al., 2019, Blommer et al., 2017). Such studies were coded as ‘traffic present, number unspecified’. In terms of SAE levels, the majority of the studies (N = 173, corresponding with 93.5 % of the deducible SAE levels) described a transition from level 3 (conditional) or level 4 (high) to level 1 (assisted) or level 0 (manual). The lowest deducibility within setting was found for mode awareness (41.3 %), which is alarming given the importance of clear communication (e.g., Carsten & Martens, 2019). In so far as communication on the automation status prior to the TOR was reported (N = 78), most of the studies used at least a symbol (N = 50; 64.1 % of the deducible sample), especially in exclusive combination with color (N = 25; 32.1 %), such as a car icon with a green road ahead in Lu et al. (2019). Regarding completeness of transfer, all driving functions were typically transferred at the same time (N = 165; 94.3 %). Drivers almost exclusively responded to transition requests through physical controls (e.g., steering wheel, pedals, buttons, levers; N = 174; 96.7 %). An exception was a dialogue based TOR described by Politis et al. (2018), aiming to increase situation awareness prior to a non-critical takeover situation. Furthermore, four studies involved a manipulation of the input modality. For example, Wintersberger et al. (2019) describe two experiments; one in which participants had to respond to a TOR by putting their hands on the steering wheel, and another in which a touch tablet was used as substitute for the steering wheel. In most cases, drivers did not have to confirm that they took over control (i.e., involvement; N = 139; 88.5 %). If drivers did not respond, mostly no fallback was implemented, meaning that a potential crash was not automatically avoided (N = 87; 75.7 %). A total of 26 studies reported that the vehicle automatically stopped (in own lane N = 15; outside own lane N = 2; lane unknown N = 9).

4. General discussion

Meta studies have largely neglected the influence of TOR design on take-over performance. The aim of this study was to inform future meta studies about the level of detail with which TOR designs are reported, by systematically reviewing academic literature with a newly postulated categorization framework. The main findings, implications, and limitations of the systematic review, along with recommendations for future research, will be presented first. Next, improvements and extensions of the framework are discussed.

4.1. Systematic review

4.1.1. Main findings & implications

Our systematic review classified a total of 391 TOR designs found in 189 academic studies. Compared to previous inventories of TOR designs (35 TORs in Mirnig et al., 2017; 31 TORs in Boelhouwer et al, 2019), the present inventory is the largest in terms of sample size as well as the number of coded variables. In general, deducibility of variables decreased when variables resided deeper within the hierarchical framework presented in Fig. 1. This decreasing order was also found in the percentage agreement between coders, suggesting that a lack of reporting fosters ambiguity when interpreting an experimental setup.

To analyze the effect of TOR design on take-over performance, it is imperative that studies investigating take-over situations describe the TOR design at a detailed level. Prospective meta studies may benefit from the finding that deducibility was high at the levels of Modality (i.e., 98.7 %, included in previous meta studies) and Class (87.1 % on average, not included so far). The same cannot be said for attributes, however. With an average attribute deducibility of 50.5 % across all deducible classes, the sample that can be included in a meta study involving TOR design at the level of attributes may be too low to reach a desirable statistical power. There are more implications of a low deducibility of TOR designs. For example, researchers intending to replicate a study may not be able to reproduce the exact same experimental setup. Lacking insights from meta studies, the impact of deviations from a former experimental setup may remain unknown. As another example, researchers may not be able to assess compliance with HMI guidelines, such as the use of contrasting colors and minimum signal-to-noise ratios to ensure detectability (e.g., Naujoks et al., 2019b).

In terms of implementation, no archetypical TOR appears to exist. Visual-auditory TORs may constitute the largest group in terms of modality, but at class level there is no clearly favorable TOR design. Auditory TORs, the second-largest group in terms of modality, features either earcons or speech. Other than noting that these classes are single bursts (earcons and speech), involving beeps or unspecified tones (earcons), or English phrases (speech), no further common themes can be derived from the multitude of coded variables. The reasons for a lack of common themes are low deducibility at the attribute level, and a large variation within attributes in case deducibility is high.

Another finding in terms of implementation is that a large part of the potential TOR design space has not been covered (or coverage is unknown due to a low deducibility). For example, almost all TORs involved a single burst, which suggests that temporal or rhythmic aspects of TORs have received little attention. Also, the classes sonification, anthropomorphism, and force feedback were not encountered, and only a single study reported auditory icons. Knowing which classes constitute a sample helps to interpret the findings of previous meta studies. For example, Zhang et al. (2019) report that unimodal visual TORs were associated with longer mean TOTs than unimodal auditory or vibrotactile TORs. This finding may be true for text, symbols, and abstract unimodal visual TORs, albeit potentially biased by text-based TORs (see Fig. 9). This finding may also be true for earcons, speech, and to a lesser extent for auditory icons (due to its low prevalence). However, the studies examined in Zhang et al. (2019) did not include TORs with sonification, nor anthropomorphism, and effects of these classes on TOT therefore remain unknown. Thus, one should be cautious making statements that generalize towards an entire modality, instead of the classes that constitute the sample.

4.1.2. Limitations & recommendations

The observation that certain classes have not been implemented (or described) and that certain attributes show little variation does not necessarily mean that implementing those classes and/or choosing other implementations on certain attributes will improve take-over performance. Such impact is largely unknown as of yet. Thus, follow-up research is recommended in which, amongst others, TOR class is systematically manipulated, involving classes that have received no attention (i.e., anthropomorphism, sonification, force feedback) or little attention (e.g., auditory icons).

There are seven factors that have or may have contributed to a lowered deducibility. First, the hierarchical framework poses restrictions in that if a TOR attribute is known, but its class is not, the attribute cannot be coded (e.g., pulse duration could belong to any auditory class). Second, attributes were at times reported using different units than what was accounted for in the coding sheet (e.g., traffic density in vehicles per hour versus vehicles per kilometer). Third, attributes (e.g., signal and background loudness) may have been unknown, but the goal of reporting these attribute (e.g., detectability) was met nonetheless. Fourth, several studies referenced to previous work when reporting a TOR implementation. In case of ambiguous references (using phrases such as ‘based on…’ without further specifications) it is unknown if and which deviations from the previous setup have been introduced. Such ambiguity should therefore be avoided when reporting an experimental setup. Seven studies unambiguously referred to previous work. Modality and class could typically be derived without consulting the referenced materials, but the possibility exists that further information may be found on attributes, setting, and/or background related variables, which means deducibility figures reported in our study may be an underestimation. Fifth, article length restrictions may have forced authors to leave out certain details about the experimental setup. Sixth, studies involving an experimental manipulation of the TOR design more likely report details on (differences between) the TOR designs than studies that do not involve such a manipulation. Seeing that many studies in our sample did not involve an experimental manipulation of the TOR design, a bias towards a lowered deducibility may have been introduced. Seventh, and related to the former factor, authors may have been unaware about the relevance of certain details for future studies when writing the manuscript (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2019). Factors 1–4 may be mitigated by adjustments in the coding scheme or framework, or by examining referenced studies. Factors 5–7, however, require more awareness about the need for detailed documentation, e.g., by optimizing guidelines for reporting an experimental setup.

A bias may have been introduced by our information sources, search strategy, eligibility criteria, and study selection method. More studies may have been found when other databases (e.g., IEEE, Scopus, Google Scholar) were consulted in addition to the information sources consulted in the present study, including more theses, books, conference papers and unpublished materials (Martín-Martín et al., 2018). Nonetheless, studies examined in the meta-analyses of Zhang et al. (2019) and Weaver and DeLucia (2022), as well as the reviews of Mirnig et al., 2017, Boelhouwer et al., 2019 were collected with similar queries as the present study, using Google Scholar, ResearchGate, PsycINFO, PsycArticles, MEDLINE, ACM Digital Library, IEEE, ScienceDirect, Scopus, as well as using snowballing techniques. Thus, indirectly, the present study made (partial) use of those information sources. We therefore expect that our sample is representative for TOR designs published in English academic literature. However, it is not complete. The meta-analysis and framework studies, each of which involved queries using several databases, were published before 2021. This means that our sample may exclude studies published in 2021 if unavailable through Web of Science. Also, studies published in languages other than English were not included. Additional databases and languages need to be included to obtain a complete sample.

Another bias may have been introduced by the possibility that multiple reports of the same study were included, such as a conference proceeding re-submitted to a journal using a different title. Dey et al. (2020) note that information about a single design is sometimes described over multiple reports. Our rationale is that if one reads a publication, one should not have to search for other potentially existing reports of the same study to get a full picture of the experimental design, unless an explicit reference to previous work is provided. Several reports referred to previous work when describing a TOR design. However, in case of ambiguous references in which the TOR design was ‘based on’ previous work, one cannot exclude the possibility that subtle differences in the experimental setup have been introduced. Judging whether such differences are large enough to speak of distinct TOR designs is prone to interpretation (Dey et al., 2020). From the perspective of deducibility, and to minimize bias introduced by interpretation, we chose to include all reports, even if they may have described the same study. By doing so, descriptive statistics on the implementation of a TOR design may have suffered from a bias due to double counting. Future meta studies need to account for such bias by applying more strict study selection criteria.

4.2. Reflection on the framework

4.2.1. Main findings & implications

The framework introduced in the present study extends previous HMI classification frameworks (Mirnig et al., 2017, Boelhouwer et al., 2019, Dey et al., 2020) and takes into account parameters required to assess HMI guidelines reported by Naujoks et al. (2019b), by introducing a set of unique classes within each modality and a set of generic attributes (e.g., location, intensity, frequency, duration) as well as class-specific attributes. Consequently, the present framework involves more variables at a finer level of detail than previous classification frameworks, allowing for detailed inventories of and comparisons between TOR designs. The increased level of detail also allows for more accurate replication of experimental setups in future studies.

A pre-requisite for inventorying and comparing TOR designs (e.g., as part of a meta-analysis on take-over performance), as well as replicating an experimental setup, is that studies actually report the details described in the framework. The notion of missing data (i.e., lowered deducibility) is not new (e.g., Joscelyn and Maickel, 1977, Cabral and Remijn, 2019). Previous inventories of TOR designs also included missing values (Mirnig et al., 2017), or used ‘unspecified’ as one of the coding options (Dey et al., 2020). Medical research typically makes use of checklists to facilitate full reporting of experimental stimuli for future replication (e.g., Sakzewski et al., 2016, Avey et al., 2016). Research on traffic safety may similarly benefit from such a checklist, which at present appears to be missing. The framework postulated in the present study and the accompanying codebook may assist in systematically reporting TOR design parameters in future studies (e.g., by including a filled out checklist as an appendix), and to create an inventory of TOR design parameters used in previous studies.

4.2.2. Limitations & recommendations

The systematic review presented here is a first exploration of the classification framework. The low interrater reliability on a number of variables indicates that clearer operational definitions may be needed. What should be realized, though, is that information on an experimental setup was gathered by researchers not involved in those studies, based on published reports only. Moreover, interrater reliability was lower at deeper levels of the framework, where information was more often found to be lacking. Interpretation of the operational definitions may be less ambiguous if studies are coded by researchers at the time they are involved in the corresponding studies, with access to (additional documents about) the experimental setup. Therefore, a follow-up study is recommended to better assess the interpretability of the operational definitions, by having researchers code their own studies.

The framework can be extended in terms of depth by including the possibility to categorize modulations of certain TOR attributes while TORs are presented, seeing that such modulations may influence take-over performance. For example, urgency can be conveyed by decreasing the inter-burst interval or inter-pulse interval (van der Heiden et al., 2017, van den Beukel et al., 2016), an approach also used by parking sensors to communicate gap size. Tuuri et al. (2011) show that urgency can also be conveyed by applying intonation to earcons (e.g., changing the pitch of a tone during a pulse). Furthermore, Imbert et al. (2014) show that animation and movement of visual notifications influence detection speed and accuracy by air traffic controllers. Possibly these effects are also true for TOR signals in an automated driving context. Additionally, certain TOR attributes may be designed to adapt to environmental conditions (e.g., a louder TOR in a noisy driving environment), and vice versa, certain environmental conditions may adapt to the presence of a TOR (e.g., pausing music prior to a TOR). Further extensions in terms of depth may include the number of TOR exposures during an experiment and whether TORs have been manipulated in terms of modality and/or class, to accommodate studies on learning effects, habituation, and potential communication of TOR reasons.

The framework can also be extended in terms of scope. The present framework and systematic review focused on the context of a takeover scenario. Other use cases involving HMI signals may be classified with relatively minor adaptations of the framework. For example, Mulvihill et al. (2021) describe four implementations of a driver state monitoring and warning systems. One of those implementations involves an ‘auditory alerting tone’ at 70 dBA, followed by a spoken message with an Australian female voice at 70 dBA and a tactile warning with 5 pulses. In our framework, this implementation would be classified as auditory-tactile (modality), with an earcon, speech, and vibration (classes). The intensity of the auditory components as well as the phrase can be deduced, but earcon frequency and duration cannot (attributes). Furthermore, the traffic density of the driving simulator is mentioned (setting), as well as the fact that participants were distracted by a visual-manual NDRT (background signals). Thus, the hierarchical structure introduced in Fig. 1 may be re-used in other use cases, except that the labels ‘Takeover’ and ‘TOR signal’ should be replaced by the corresponding use case and main signal names, respectively. Additional research is needed to determine to what degree individual variables within each block of the hierarchical structure apply, and if additional levels within categorical variables are required in alternative use cases.

When considering concurrent use cases (e.g., a takeover scenario in combination with driver state monitoring and warning system), simultaneous presentation of signals originating from separate sub-systems may become an issue for discriminability, detectability, and understandability. For example, two sounds with similar acoustic properties may be perceived as a single auditory object (Bregman, 1994), and accuracy in identifying individual sounds decreases when more sounds are presented concurrently (Nees & Walker, 2011). Naujoks et al. (2019b) present several guidelines related to discriminability and detectability of visual, auditory, and tactile HMI signals, including advisory ranges for pulse duration and frequency, as well as raising the intensity of auditory signals above noise produced by a vehicle in motion. However, no guidelines are presented on avoiding (perceptual) confusion between multiple signals. In the present framework, detectability and discriminability of a single signal can be examined relative to all background signals. In the takeover use case, signals related to driver monitoring and warning systems may be part of the background. Vice versa, in the use case of driver monitoring and warning, TOR signals may be part of the background. Thus, our framework may assist the (design or) evaluation of an environment in which multiple signals are presented concurrently.

Finally, the framework could be extended to facilitate principles of inclusive design. For example, restrictions in sight, hearing and touch may limit the detectability of a TOR, which otherwise would have been perfectly detectable for drivers without such restrictions. Furthermore, cultural differences have been shown to influence, e.g., meaning attributed to colors (Tham et al., 2020) and HMI usability (Khan & Williams, 2014). Adding participant characteristics to the framework (e.g., as part of the ‘Setting’) could facilitate future meta-analysis to investigate potential moderating effects of the population on the relation between TOR design and takeover performance, and subsequent design guidelines that may result from such meta-analysis.

5. Conclusion

Meta studies on factors contributing to take-over performance did not systematically include TOR design, other than the modality at which TORs are presented. A detailed understanding of the influence of TOR design on take-over performance is therefore lacking. The present study postulated a classification framework to facilitate a detailed description of TOR designs. The framework was operationalized into a coding sheet to perform a systematic review on TOR designs in academic literature. The systematic review revealed that no predominant TOR design exists, and a considerable part of the available design space has not yet been explored. Moreover, the deducibility of reported information on TOR designs appears to be inversely related with the level of detail at which TORs are examined. The classification framework and the corresponding coding sheet could support systematic reporting in future work. If the devil is indeed in the details, subsequent meta-analysis will provide a better understanding about the impact of TOR design on take-over performance, which in turn can support implementation of safe and effective TORs in our vehicles.

Abstract visual shapes or other forms of light-based or non-light-based communication devices that use metaphors, or signals that aim at communicating intuitively via a nonconcrete, open-to-interpretation interface that is neither anthropomorphic, textual, or symbolic.Yes, No, Unknown, Not applicableA class is not applicable if the corresponding modality is not implemented.
Auditory speechDoes the auditory TOR have a speech component? Prerecorded natural voicings or synthetic voicings.Yes, No, Unknown, Not applicableA class is not applicable if the corresponding modality is not implemented.
Auditory iconDoes the auditory TOR have an auditory icon component? Brief sounds that have some a priori association with their referent object, event, or process. The relationship between the sound and its meaning in the interface can range from quite literal (e.g., the sound of crackling flames to represent an engine fire) to more metaphorical (e.g., the sound of crumpling paper to represent a computer file being deleted).Yes, No, Unknown, Not applicableA class is not applicable if the corresponding modality is not implemented.
Auditory earconDoes the auditory TOR have an earcon component? Earcons are abstract, artificial sounds that bear no ecological relationship to the represented process or event (e.g., a single 'beep' or 'tone').Yes, No, Unknown, Not applicableA class is not applicable if the corresponding modality is not implemented.
Auditory sonificationDoes the auditory TOR have a sonification component? The use of non-speech audio to display quantitative data (e.g., geiger counters, parking assist systems).Yes, No, Unknown, Not applicableA class is not applicable if the corresponding modality is not implemented.
Tactile vibrationDoes the tactile TOR have a vibration component? (e.g., vibration implemented in the seat or steering wheel)Yes, No, Unknown, Not applicableA class is not applicable if the corresponding modality is not implemented.
Tactile force feedbackDoes the tactile TOR have a force feedback component? (e.g., resistance applied to the pedals)Yes, No, Unknown, Not applicableA class is not applicable if the corresponding modality is not implemented.

Appendix D:. Interrater reliability

In general there are two approaches to assess whether coders have the same interpretation of a codebook. In one approach, all materials are processed by at least two coders, after which disagreements between coders are resolved (e.g., Mirnig et al., 2017, Dey et al., 2020). Measures of agreement are typically not calculated. In another approach, a sample of the materials is processed by multiple coders (e.g., Zhang et al., 2019), after which measures of agreement may be calculated. This second approach was chosen in the present study, due to the relatively large sample size and number of variables, as well as the opportunity to gain insights into the clarity of the operational definitions of the codebook.

The agreement between the coders was assessed in three rounds using a random sample of 5 studies per round of testing (without duplicates of formerly coded studies). Scores resulting from Round 1 and Round 2 were used to facilitate plenary discussions on understanding causes for disagreement, occasionally leading to refinements of definitions and operationalizations in the codebook. Individual bulk coding of the studies started after Round 2. Finally, a third interrater reliability test round (Round 3) was performed to probe whether the joint interpretation of the codebook was constant and sufficient throughout the coding process.

Percentage agreement for each variable was calculated as the proportion of papers at which all coders agreed. The average percentage agreement was then calculated across variables belonging to the same group (i.e., TOR Modality, TOR Class, TOR Attribute, Background signals, and Setting). Starting at the highest hierarchical level for TOR signals, for each modality (e.g., Visual), disagreement across the coders on whether a modality was used in a particular paper resulted in exclusion of that paper from further analysis at the level of TOR Class (e.g., Text, Symbol, Abstract, Anthropomorphic), because missing values would be introduced otherwise. Likewise, if coders disagreed on the class(es) used in a particular paper, then that paper was not further analyzed at the level of TOR Attributes for the classes at which disagreement was found. Previous studies have used a criterion of 80 % above which a variable is said to have an adequate reliability to be considered for subsequent analysis using statistical models (e.g., Varotto et al., 2021). In our study, we have used the 80 % threshold as an indicator for adequate reliability, but seeing that no further statistical models were constructed, we have chosen to describe all variables, including variables with a percentage agreement below 80 %.

For each group of variables the average agreement across coders is depicted in Fig. D.1. For TOR signals, the agreement was highest for Modality, followed by Class, and lowest for Attribute. This order suggests that coding a paper becomes more difficult the more one zooms in. In Round 2, i.e., prior to individually coding the bulk of the papers, the average agreement was above 80 % for all groups, except Background signals. By the end of the coding process, the average agreement showed a decrease in all groups, with an average agreement below 80 % for Attribute, Setting, and Background signals.

Within Attributes, variables relating to the number of bursts and pulses most often yielded disagreement between coders in Round 3 (but not in Round 2). Such disagreement typically concerned whether the number of bursts or pulses was known or unknown.

For Setting, underlying variables with an agreement below 80 % during Round 2 and/or Round 3 were Traffic density (both rounds), Fallback (one round), Involvement (both rounds), and Mode awareness indication (both rounds). The percentage agreement on Fallback and Mode awareness (and also their deducibility, see below) was surprisingly low, considering that the operational definitions were copied from Mirnig et al. (2017). In that study, all papers were coded by two researchers separately, after which disagreements were corrected. Mirnig et al. (2017) do not report how often disagreement occurred, which means it is not possible to make a comparison with the percentage agreement found in the present study. Nonetheless, our findings indicate that Fallback and Mode awareness may require a clearer definition.

Background signals showed an agreement below 80 % in Round 2 on the underlying variables specifying the presence of visual and auditory background signals and whether auditory background noise was present. By Round 3 this was resolved, except for the presence of visual background signals. Furthermore, coders disagreed on all types of NDRT-involvement (e.g., manual, visual, auditory; here interpreted as background signals due to potential masking of and distraction from TORs) in Round 3.
